subsection.title: Tangent slope
subsection.p: The derivative has a geometric meaning. It is the slope of the tangent line.
For a curve y=f(x), the secant line through (a,f(a)) and (a+h,f(a+h)) has slope
As h\to 0, the second point approaches the first. If the secant slopes approach a single number, that number is the slope of the tangent line at (a,f(a)).

paragraphs.title: A tangent line can cross the curve
paragraphs.p: It is tempting to say that a tangent line is a line that touches the graph at one point and does not cross it. That picture works for some curves, but it is not a definition.
For example, let f(x)=x^3. At x=0,
So the tangent line at (0,0) is y=0. But the graph of y=x^3 crosses this line at the origin. The tangent line is still correct because its slope is the limiting secant slope.

subsection.title: The derivative as a limit
subsection.p: The derivative is a limit of slopes:
This formula has three layers.
First, the quotient \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is an average rate of change over an interval.
Second, the limit h\to 0 shrinks the interval toward a single input.
Third, the result f'(a), if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change at a.
The limit must exist as one finite number. If the slopes approach different values from different sides, there is no derivative.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: the corner in |x|
paragraphs.p: Let f(x)=|x|. Try to find f'(0).
The right-side slopes approach 1. The left-side slopes approach -1. There is no single limiting slope. Therefore f'(0) does not exist.

figure.caption: At a corner, the left and right limiting slopes can disagree. Then the derivative does not exist.

paragraphs.p: The graph has a sharp corner at the origin. The corner is not the real reason the derivative fails; it is the picture of the reason. The reason is that the limiting slopes do not approach one common value.

statement.p: The derivative at a exists only when \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} exists as a finite number.
If the left and right slopes disagree, or if the slopes grow without bound, then f'(a) does not exist.

subsection.p: One derivative gives one slope at one point. But a curve has many points. If we let the point a move, the derivative itself becomes a new function. That new function will tell us how the whole graph is changing.
